initial_conversion.migration: lossless native packaging of approved H.R.5408 decisions

changes.before:
The bill covers bargaining for a first contract after a union is newly recognized or certified. If there is no agreement 90 days after bargaining starts, either side may ask for mediation from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. agency that provides mediators: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [1] A mediator cannot decide the dispute. If there is still no agreement 30 days after that request, the dispute goes to arbitration, where a panel decides: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1].

The panel has “one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [1] If a side does not choose its member, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [1] The panel majority’s decision binds both sides for two years unless both agree in writing to change it. Either waiting period can be longer only if both sides agree.

Under the law in force on June 9, 2026, there is no such route. The duty to bargain “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [2].

The panel route applies only to a first contract, not to later contracts. The bill sets no deadline for the panel’s decision: “it does not limit the timeline of arbitration.” [3]

Under current law, neither side has to agree to anything. Under the bill, either side can start the route to a panel after the waiting periods, and neither side can stop the panel by refusing to choose its member. More time needs both sides’ agreement.

changes.before:
Under existing law, upon reaching a good-faith impasse, “the NLRA entitles an employer to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer.” [1] The NLRA is the main U.S. private-sector labor law. The bill adds a duty “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2].

Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe reads this duty as one that “extends indefinitely beyond the point when the parties reach a good faith impasse to the date the parties reach agreement.” [3] He adds that it “applies not just to first contracts, but rather to all employers and all contracts.” [3]

This reading comes from law-firm analyses, not a court ruling. The duty keeps both good and bad current terms, so it can stop an employer from either cutting them or raising them on its own. The sources give no figure for how often employers make such changes today.

changes.before: The Heritage Foundation, a policy research group, states: “Currently, nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” [1] The bill says “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute” [2] and provides no member vote on that decision. This applies only to disputes a panel decides. The union chooses one of the three panel members.

changes.before: Sick leave and infection. “Paid sick leave benefits allow workers to stay home and visit a healthcare provider when ill.” [4] A U.S. study comparing states found: “We find clear evidence that sick pay mandates reduce ILI infection rates at the population level.” [5] ILI means flu-like illness.

changes.before: Time for worship. Sunday worship is an established Christian custom, and passing on faith needs regular family time: “For children to absorb God’s truths, regular times of family Bible study, devotion and worship are important.” [6] Two separate routes protect that time. First, with current terms held during talks, the bill protects established Sunday and holiday arrangements against changes an employer would otherwise impose after a deadlock. For example, the 2021–25 contract at Kroger, a grocery company, gives certain groups of longtime workers this rule: “Sunday and holiday work shall be voluntary and rotated among qualified employees who are available for such work.” [7] Such existing arrangements are protected against changes an employer would otherwise impose after a deadlock. Second, first contracts can add religious scheduling rules and advance notice of schedules, which lets families plan regular worship and teaching.

changes.before: Care workers and infection. First-contract arbitration gives workers a “guaranteed path to get the benefits of a union contract” [1]. Longmont United nurses won “the first acute care private-sector contract for RNs in the state of Colorado.” [2] It included “Health and safety provisions to ensure nurses get the highest level of personal protective equipment when caring for patients with infectious diseases.” [2] Guidance from the CDC, the U.S. public health agency, lists “use of gloves, gown, mask, eye protection, or face shield, depending on the anticipated exposure” [3]. With such terms, care workers get protections that an employer cannot block just by refusing to sign any contract.

changes.before: Oversight and enforcement. A union contract can give workers a regular role in environmental oversight. The 2018 U.S. Steel contract requires “A Joint Environmental Sub-Committee of the Joint Safety and Health Committee” [3] at each location, which “will meet regularly to discuss environmental issues affecting the Company and to make appropriate recommendations.” [3] The company must let that group review “all non confidential environmental reports, monitoring results, analyses, materials received from the EPA and other agencies” [3], and must “comply with all applicable laws and regulations concerning the health and safety of Employees at work and the protection of the environment.” [3] The EPA is the U.S. environmental agency. Workers can enforce these duties: “the Union may process grievances through the grievance procedure, including arbitration” [3]. These terms give workers information, a voice and a way to enforce environmental duties.

changes.before: The required duty to bargain concerns safety and health: “the other side must bargain in good faith over safety and health issues, including SWA.” [4] SWA means workers’ authority to stop unsafe work. “Because there is no law mandating SWA, the SWA process is specific to an employer or workplace.” [4] The environmental wording comes from the Delaware City process, and environment-only coverage is not shown to be a required subject. This does not answer stop-work terms for hazards to workers that would also prevent environmental harm.

This does not answer stop-work terms for hazards to workers that would also prevent environmental harm.

changes.before: Green workplace programs. A guide to green bargaining explains that U.S. employers and unions “are still free to bargain over” climate goals [1]. Its contract models include “building efficiency improvements and recycling and composting programs” [1]. U.S. Steel’s contract requires joint work to “identify, analyze, and make recommendations regarding ways to conserve energy, improve energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions” [3]. Minneapolis janitors won a “contract that included funding for a Labor-Management Cooperation Fund for a green education initiative” [5]. The IPCC, the United Nations climate science panel, finds that “Hundreds of local losses of species have been driven by increases in the magnitude of heat extremes” [6].

changes.before: Marriage. The Southern Baptist Convention teaches: “Marriage is a lifelong covenant between one man and one woman” [7], and calls for “the overturning of laws and court rulings, including Obergefell v. Hodges, that defy God’s design for marriage and family” [7]. Obergefell is the U.S. Supreme Court decision recognizing same-sex marriage. The AFL-CIO lobbied for the opposite policy: “The AFL-CIO urges you to vote in support of HR 8404, the Respect for Marriage Act.” [9] AFT confirms it “is affiliated with American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations” [3].

changes.before: A Canadian study found: “FCA reduces first agreement work stoppage incidence by at least 50 percent.” [1] FCA means first-contract arbitration. The study says Canadian labor laws are “modeled on U.S. labor law.” [1] It explains the result as “creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement” [1]. Separately, a binding decision gives the two sides an ordinary way to end a dispute without a stoppage. So the bill would reduce, at least somewhat, how often first-contract bargaining leads to a strike or lockout. This concerns how often stoppages happen, and it does not assume that the 50 percent figure applies.

changes.before: Safety rules. OSHA, the U.S. workplace safety agency, explains: “The process described in these recommended practices can, and should, be tailored to the needs of each workplace.” [3] An imposed contract lasts two years unless changed by “written consent of the parties.” [2] A safety rule that misses a workplace’s actual hazards can leave workers exposed to injury.

changes.before: Schedules, sick leave and coverage also affect health. NIOSH, a U.S. workplace-health agency, explains: “Work-related factors that can contribute to fatigue include scheduling practices, such as night shifts or extended hours, that can interfere with sleep.” [9] “Fatigued workers might take more risks that lead to injury or errors.” [9] The danger reaches road users “when fatigued workers drive on public roads.” [9] NIOSH also explains: “Access to paid sick leave might reduce the pressure to work while sick out of fear of losing income.” [10] It found that “workers with access to paid sick leave were 28% less likely overall to suffer nonfatal occupational injuries than workers without access to paid sick leave.” [10] Having insurance does not ensure affordable care. The Commonwealth Fund’s 2024 survey found: “Nearly three of five (57%) underinsured adults said they avoided getting needed health care because of its cost” [11]. Workers at Conagra, a food company, rejected a proposed contract whose terms failed to address concerns about “forced overtime and double shifts” [12] and which “would have resulted in higher health insurance costs” [12]. In a contract a panel sets, workers lose a way to reject tiring schedules, sick leave or health benefits they find too limited.

changes.before: Essential services. The agency describes its role: “Our mediators work tirelessly to minimize and prevent disruptions affecting utilities, health care, public safety and security.” [6] The National Restaurant Association, a business group, warns: “The FLCA also assumes a significant expansion in federal mediation capacity that has not been funded.” [7] FLCA is the Faster Labor Contracts Act, this bill. New required cases would compete for the resources used to prevent disruptions to power and health care.

changes.before: Strikes for green terms. Employers seek strike bans in first contracts: “management will demand a contract clause barring strikes while the agreement is in effect.” [7] Today “Nothing in the NLRA, however, requires a union to agree to a no-strike clause.” [7] Lawyers describe the panel’s “authority to determine all terms of the parties’ first CBA” [8]. A CBA is a collective bargaining agreement, or contract. Green demands can concern daily work; a janitors’ union sought a “training program for Green Technicians (including $0.20 differential) and expanded use of green cleaning.” [9] Strike pressure helps: “the companies will simply try to ignore those demands—unless the union is willing to sacrifice and ultimately strike.” [10] A binding award can limit stoppages used to press such demands in either of two ways. The award itself ends the first-contract bargaining in which workers could strike for such terms, or it could impose a strike ban they never accepted.

changes.before: Current law does not ensure terms both sides accept. After a real deadlock, “an employer does not violate the Act by making unilateral changes that are reasonably comprehended within his pre-impasse proposals” [11]. Agreement on terms is also a different test from understanding the people who propose them. The bill requires parties to “make every reasonable effort to conclude and sign a collective bargaining agreement” [2]. Canadian research reports: “Despite this, FCA is not accessed frequently and it is even rarer for a first contract (in whole or in part) to be imposed.” [12] FCA means first-contract arbitration. Those Canadian systems also had a rule stopping strikes that this bill does not state. One side’s refusal to extend talks after sincere bargaining does not itself show less willingness to understand the other group.

changes.after: This bill would change U.S. labor law for workers who have newly formed a union. An employer would have to begin talks soon after the union asks. If the two sides cannot agree on a first contract, either side can ask a federal agency for mediation. If mediation does not produce an agreement, a three-person panel decides, and both sides must follow the panel’s decision for two years. The bill would also require current pay and working conditions to stay in place during talks and would keep an employer’s duty to bargain until workers remove the union in an election.
